Italy
ĭt´ȧ-lĭ
n. (the peninsula of Rome; the destination of Paul's appeal and of his last voyage)
Latin Italia. In the New Testament the name marks a direction rather than a culture — the place the gospel was travelling toward from the day Paul said he must also see Rome.

Biblical Definition

Italy enters Acts through an expulsion: “a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome)” (Act 18:2). It returns as a sentence: “when it was determined that we should sail into Italy, they delivered Paul and certain other prisoners unto one named Julius, a centurion of Augustus' band” (Act 27:1), and “the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing into Italy; and he put us therein” (Act 27:6). After shipwreck, brethren were found on the road and “so we went toward Rome” (Act 28:14). The epistle to the Hebrews closes with a greeting from there: “They of Italy salute you” (Heb 13:24).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a centurion as a military officer among the Romans who commanded a hundred men, and a prisoner as one who is confined in a prison or held in custody.

expand to see more

CENTURION, n. Among the Romans, a military officer who commanded a hundred men, a centenary or century.

PRISONER, n. One who is confined in a prison by legal arrest or warrant; also, a person under arrest or in custody.

APPEAL, n. In law, the removal of a cause or suit from an inferior to a superior tribunal.

Key Scripture

Act 18:2 — "And found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome:) and came unto them."

Act 27:1 — "And when it was determined that we should sail into Italy, they delivered Paul and certain other prisoners unto one named Julius, a centurion of Augustus' band."

Act 28:14 — "Where we found brethren, and were desired to tarry with them seven days: and so we went toward Rome."

Heb 13:24 — "Salute all them that have the rule over you, and all the saints. They of Italy salute you."

Modern Corruption

An emperor's expulsion order put Aquila and Priscilla in Corinth exactly when Paul arrived there, which is how Acts tells the story of providence.

expand to see more

Acts 18:2 gives a persecution and a provision in one sentence. Claudius commanded all Jews to depart from Rome; Aquila and Priscilla, therefore, were in Corinth, of the same craft as Paul, when he came there alone and with little money. They housed him, worked with him, travelled with him to Ephesus, taught Apollos the way of God more perfectly, and hosted a church in their house. An imperial edict aimed at scattering a people delivered the two co-workers Paul most needed to the exact city where he needed them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Paul stated from Rome itself: the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel. He had wanted to see Rome for years and arrived as a prisoner after a shipwreck, and the palace guard heard the gospel as a result. Acts ends with him in his own hired house, preaching the kingdom of God with all confidence, no man forbidding him — and the last word of the book in Greek is that adverb, unhinderedly. The chain was real. It did not slow the word.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Italia (G2482), Italy; hekatontarches (G1543), centurion; akolutos (G209), without hindrance.

expand to see more

Greek Italia (G2482) — Italy; Acts 18:2, 27:1, 27:6, Hebrews 13:24.

Greek hekatontarches (G1543) — centurion; Acts 27:1, 10:1, Matthew 8:5.

Greek akolutos (G209) — without hindrance, freely; Acts 28:31 only.

Greek prokope (G4297) — furtherance, progress; Philippians 1:12, 1:25.

Greek desmos (G1199) — bond, chain; Philippians 1:13, Acts 20:23.

Usage

"“Lately come from Italy” — an expulsion that supplied Paul with fellow workers."

"“We should sail into Italy” — the apostle delivered to a centurion."

"“They of Italy salute you” — a church in the capital."
